newsitem.title: USA: SEC chief defends new derivatives rules.
newsitem.headline: SEC chief defends new derivatives rules.

text.p: Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Arthur Levitt defended his agency's new rules that require public companies to disclose more information about the derivatives they own.

"People buy (Proctor & Gamble) stock because they want to invest in a soapmaker; if they want a business that plays derivatives full time, they will buy Salomon Inc," Levitt said in a letter to Phil Gramm, the Texas Republican who chairs the subcommittee of Senate Banking Committee which oversees the SEC in an April 22 letter.
Most derivatives, financial instruments whose value is based on or "derived from" the value of an underlying instrument, are linked to interest rates or currencies.
Concern about their risks arose when many companies and some municipalities lost millions of dollars when interest rates shifted in 1994.
"Problem is, it's not easy to know whether a company is using derivatives on a large scale," Levitt wrote.

His comments follow a scathing report Gramm's committee submitted to the agency earlier this week that called the new disclosure rules burdensome. The bi-partisan report said the new disclosure would "present to investors a distorted and misleading picture of company conditions and activities."

The agency earlier this year approved its rules amidst widesprad industry disapproval. At that time it said it would phase in the new reporting over 1997 and 1998, requiring companies to disclose the value of their derivatives holdings and any potential risks.

Improved disclosure became an issue of concern for the agency when big companies like Procter & Gamble Co., Gibson Greetings and Eastman Kodak Co suffered huge losses as a result of soured derivatives investments.

But nonetheless, in his most recent letter, Levitt agreed to review the rules after one year, rather than in three years. "We expect to complete our review of the first set of registrants by mid-June 1998," Levitt wrote.
But this may not be enough for Gramm and other lawmakers who want the agency to test the rules out on a smaller group of firms before imposing them.
